Eggs of the Mediterranean killifish Aphanius fasciatus, when incubated at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], typically hatch after 11 days [ab = 11 days], a developmental period characteristic of cyprinodontids inhabiting shallow, warm coastal lagoons. The newly emerged prolarvae are minute, with a total length at birth of 0.51 cm [Lb = 0.51 cm], reflecting the comparatively small egg size of this species. Following chorion rupture, the yolk-sac larva remains non-feeding for a brief interval, relying entirely on endogenous reserves until mouth gape opening enables the first exogenous feeding. This rapid transition from lecithotrophy to exotrophic nutrition is an adaptation to the variable prey availability typical of hypersaline environments. The prolonged incubation period at 23 °C relative to some congeners suggests a thermal optimum for embryonic development that aligns with the summer water temperatures of the species' native habitat. Field observations from the Stagnone di Marsala indicate that the timing of eclosion is closely synchronized with seasonal phytoplankton blooms, ensuring adequate food resources for the onset of larval feeding.

As juvenile fish grow and approach sexual maturation, they reach a total length at puberty of 2.02 cm [Lp = 2.02 cm], a metric derived from females collected in the Stagnone di Marsala during 2010 and 2011. At this developmental stage, the sub-adult individuals have attained a wet weight at puberty of 0.116 grams [Wwp = 0.116 grams], reflecting the modest body size that characterizes this killifish species. The onset of gonad maturation occurs relatively early in life, with first spawning recorded at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] when water temperatures approach 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This age at first reproduction is consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy common to small-bodied teleosts inhabiting seasonal wetlands. The initiation of reproductive activity coincides with the spring warming period, when increasing photoperiod and temperature trigger the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Females during this period begin vitellogenesis, producing clutches that will be deposited on submerged vegetation.

Females of Aphanius fasciatus produce approximately 1.4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 1.4 eggs per clutch] , with a spawning frequency of approximately 1 event per day [F_R_i = approximately 1 event per day] when maintained at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], based on fecundity-length relationships derived from the Stagnone di Marsala population. This maximum reproductive rate reflects the high fecundity typical of small, short-lived cyprinodontids that invest heavily in early reproduction. The spawning season extends over several months, with gravid individuals releasing demersal, adhesive eggs that attach to aquatic macrophytes. The daily egg output is influenced by female body size and nutritional condition, with larger females contributing disproportionately to total population fecundity. Field surveys indicate that the reproductive window spans from late spring through early autumn, allowing multiple spawning events within a single season. The trade-off between current reproductive effort and future survival is evident in the relatively rapid decline in condition observed in post-spawning females.

The ultimate total length attained by females in the Stagnone di Marsala population is 7.06 cm [Li = 7.06 cm], representing the asymptotic body size achieved after several growing seasons. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight recorded for these same individuals is 7.46 grams [Wwi = 7.46 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established during the 2010-2011 sampling campaign. Adult females reach this maximum recorded body mass after approximately two to three years of growth, after which somatic investment plateaus while reproductive allocation increases. The length-weight relationship for this population conforms to the typical allometric pattern observed in the genus Aphanius, with females generally attaining larger sizes than males. This sexual size dimorphism is linked to the fecundity advantage of larger body volume, which accommodates larger ovarian masses. Comparative data from other Mediterranean populations suggest slight variation in asymptotic size, likely reflecting local productivity gradients.

The maximum recorded longevity for Mediterranean killifish in the Stagnone di Marsala is 6 years [am = 6 years] when kept at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], indicating a life span typical of small cyprinodontids inhabiting stable lagoon environments. This species exhibits a relatively slow pace of life for its body size, with individuals reaching their ultimate body dimensions before mid-life. Post-reproductive senescence manifests as a gradual decline in body condition and fecundity during the final years of life. The trade-off between early reproduction and somatic maintenance is evident in the reduced growth rates observed after the first spawning season. Natural mortality in this population is primarily driven by predation from piscivorous birds and larger fish, as well as periodic desiccation events in shallow habitats. The combination of early maturation, moderate fecundity, and a multi-year reproductive window allows Aphanius fasciatus to maintain stable populations despite stochastic environmental fluctuations characteristic of Mediterranean coastal wetlands.
